short: What the system currently looks like, as observed rather than assumed.
long: Reported by the components doing the work rather than assumed by whoever asked for it. The gap between this and desired state is the only thing a control loop acts on.

short: Something that repeatedly observes state, compares it to what is wanted, and acts.
long: Kubernetes is a collection of these rather than one program working through a plan. They run independently, and none of them assumes it was the last thing to change anything.

short: What the system is supposed to look like.
long: You write it down and it stays written down. Nothing about it changes when reality drifts away from it.

short: Look at what is wanted, look at what exists, act on the difference, then look again.
long: The loop the whole system is built from. It reads the current state rather than a stream of instructions, so an event that arrives twice or never arrives at all changes nothing.

short: An isolated process running from an image.
A packaged filesystem and start command that a container is created from.
long: The image is immutable and is identified by a tag or a digest. Anything that has to differ between environments should stay out of it.

short: One interchangeable copy of a workload.
long: Interchangeable is the important word. If any copy is as good as any other, the system is free to delete one and start another somewhere else.

short: A set of machines that Kubernetes manages as one pool of compute.
long: A cluster is a control plane plus the nodes it schedules work onto. You talk to the cluster, not to individual machines.

short: The components that decide what should run and where.
long: The API server, scheduler, and controller manager. It holds desired state and continuously drives the cluster toward it.

short: A single machine, virtual or physical, that runs workloads.
long: Each node runs a kubelet and a container runtime. The control plane places pods onto nodes; the node is responsible for actually running them.

short: You describe the end state you want, not the steps to reach it.
long: You submit an object saying "three replicas of this image". Kubernetes works out the difference from reality and closes the gap.

short: A YAML or JSON file describing a Kubernetes object.
A scope for object names within a cluster.
long: Two namespaces can each hold a Deployment named web. Namespaces scope most objects, but not cluster-wide ones such as nodes.

short: A record in the Kubernetes API describing a piece of desired state.
long: It has a kind, a name, a spec saying what you want, and later a status saying what is. Creating one changes nothing by itself, and a controller acting on it is what changes something.

short: A process running one reconciliation loop for one kind of object.
The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share a network namespace and storage.
long: Containers in a pod share an IP address and can talk over localhost. Pods are disposable by design, and you rarely create them by hand.

short: An object that keeps a stated number of identical pods running, and updates them safely.
long: A deployment owns replicasets. Changing the pod template creates a new replicaset and shifts pods over gradually, which is what makes a rollout a rollout.

short: Replacing pods with a new version incrementally, so the service stays up.
Keeps a fixed number of identical pods alive.
Like a deployment, but each pod keeps a stable identity and its own storage.
long: Pods are numbered and started in order, and each one gets its own persistent volume claim that survives a restart.

short: The default service type: reachable only from inside the cluster.
A key/value tag attached to an object, used for grouping and selection.
A label query that decides which pods an object applies to.
A stable name and address for a changing set of pods.
long: Pods come and go with new IPs. A service gives them one virtual IP and DNS name, and load balances across whichever pods currently match its selector.

short: Rules for routing external HTTP traffic to services inside the cluster.
long: An ingress object is inert on its own. An ingress controller watches those objects and configures a real proxy to match.

short: Non-secret configuration data, kept outside the container image.
long: Mount it as files or inject it as environment variables. The same image can then run in staging and production unchanged.

short: Like a ConfigMap, but for sensitive values and handled more carefully.
long: Base64 encoding is not encryption. Secrets are only as private as the cluster's RBAC and encryption-at-rest settings make them.

short: A directory made available to a pod's containers.
A piece of storage in the cluster, with a lifetime independent of any pod.
A pod's request for storage of a given size and access mode.
long: The claim is what a workload references. Kubernetes binds it to a matching volume, provisioning one on demand if a StorageClass says how.

short: A named recipe for provisioning storage automatically.
The control plane component that picks which node a new pod should run on.
long: It filters nodes that cannot fit the pod, then scores the rest on resource fit, spread, and affinity rules.

short: The agent on each node that starts and supervises the node's pods.
The system is not always correct, but something is always working on it.
long: A reconciler moves a system toward its desired state rather than putting it there. Between the moment reality diverges and the moment it matches again there is a window where the system is wrong and converging at the same time. Asking whether the gap is closing is usually more useful than asking whether it is closed.
